name: Choice-supportive bias
statement: People are said to remember a chosen option as having had more of the good features, and fewer of the bad ones, than it really did.
meaning: The claim is about memory rather than taste. Two options are described by lists of features, one is picked, and later the rememberer has to say which option each feature belonged to. Mather, Shafir and Johnson's proposal is that when the source of a remembered feature is unclear, the knowledge of what was chosen fills the gap. A pleasant feature is credited to the option taken, an unpleasant one to the option refused. The inference is reasonable, since the chosen option probably was the better one, and it produces a record of the decision that is tidier than the decision was. Attitude change after choice is a separate literature. This one is about who gets the credit for a fact.

origin.who: Mara Mather, Eldar Shafir and Marcia K. Johnson
origin.note: The paper named choice-supportive source monitoring and supplied the paradigm still in use. Mather and Johnson published the companion ageing study in Psychology and Aging the same year. The 2000 paper places itself after older work on selective memory for decision-supporting information, citing Davidson and Kiesler's 1964 job-candidate study and Greene's 1981 detective-story study, and notes that neither asked which option a remembered fact belonged to.

evidence: Four hypothetical scenarios were run as questionnaires: two job candidates, two blind dates and two roommates, the last in a choice version and a rejection version. Each option carried a list of positive and negative features, pretested so that on average 21 of 22 raters agreed on the valence of each. Participants picked one option, spent 5 to 45 minutes on unrelated tasks, then saw the features intermixed with new ones and said which option each had belonged to, or that it was new. Scores were normalised within each scenario, so a participant counted as biased only relative to other participants facing the same lists. Mean asymmetry scores were 0.22 for job candidates, t(141) = 2.73, p < .01, with 142 participants; 0.22 for dating, t(74) = 1.99, p < .05, with 75; 0.35 for the first roommate scenario, t(76) = 3.26, p < .01, with 77; and 0.44 for the second roommate choice, t(171) = 5.76, p < .001, with 172. The 207 people asked to reject a roommate rather than choose one scored 0.28, t(206) = 4.56, p < .001. The bias was carried by positive features. In the second roommate scenario it reached 0.39 for positive items and 0.16 for negative ones, F(1, 377) = 15.76, p < .001. It appeared for new features that had belonged to neither option, which is the finding the authors use to place part of the distortion at retrieval rather than at encoding.

replication.headline: Three independent groups have found the misattribution effect with source-recognition tests, and one showed it follows a false belief about which option was picked. The claim that it grows with age has failed four times.
replication.detail: Lind, Visentini, Mäntylä and Del Missier reviewed the field in 2017 and found twelve papers meeting their criteria. Their verdict on the core effect: none of the studies that looked for choice-supportive misattribution failed to find it. Their verdict on everything else: the evidence for choice-supportive fact distortion, false memory and selective forgetting is weak, and the effect has been shown almost entirely with recognition tests rather than recall. Henkel and Mather ran the paradigm over a two-day delay with 80 undergraduates and got an asymmetry score of 0.28, SE = 0.06, t(79) = 4.63, p < .001. Their second experiment answers the obvious objection that people simply chose what they already preferred. Forty-eight participants returned a week later and were told, falsely for two of the four scenarios, which option they had picked. Memory attributions followed the false reminder as strongly as the true one, 0.50 against 0.47, with no reliable difference, t(47) = 0.28. Choice alone is not the trigger. Mather, Shafir and Johnson found the bias in people who chose, 0.10, SE = 0.04, but not in people simply assigned an option, -0.07, SE = 0.04, F(1, 92) = 7.69, p < .01. Benney and Henkel, testing 172 adults, found it in a free-choice group and in a group told the assignment had been made in their best interest, and not in a group told the assignment was random. The ageing claim is the part that has not held. Mather and Johnson gave four scenarios to 54 younger adults and 108 adults aged 64 to 83, and scored 0.12 for the younger group, 0.41 for older adults tested after 30 minutes and 0.42 for older adults tested after two days. The younger group's score sat above zero only after being asked to review how they had felt, 0.41 against -0.07 for no review. Lind and colleagues record that Queen and Hess, Hess and Kotter-Grühn, Hess, Queen and Patterson, and Depping and Freund all found older adults no more choice-supportive than younger ones.

study.cite: Henkel, L. A., & Mather, M. (2007). Memory attributions for choices: How beliefs shape our memories. Journal of Memory and Language, 57(2), 163-176.

limits: Every study in the review used hypothetical options on paper. Nobody has run the paradigm on a purchase somebody actually made, and the original authors write that real decisions may carry richer memories in which misattribution is less likely. Recognition is doing almost all the work: Lind and colleagues report that free and cued recall have barely been tried, and that Depping and Freund, who used free recall, found no choice-supportive memory in their choice groups at all. That is the only null in the set. No preregistered replication and no multi-laboratory attempt was located in this search, which covered Crossref, Europe PMC, Semantic Scholar citation lists and web search. The literature is small and the authors overlap: Mather appears on four of the twelve papers, Henkel on two, Hess on three. Martina Lind's 2019 Trento doctoral thesis, titled 'Choice-supportive misremembering: A robust phenomenon?', is the obvious place to look next; its repository was returning server errors throughout this search and it was not read. The Depping and Freund null and the four ageing failures are reported here as Lind and colleagues describe them, not from the papers themselves. Asymmetry scores are normalised within a scenario and are not a standardised effect size, so the numbers above compare across these studies and nowhere else.
misreadings: The bias is usually retold as feeling better about a purchase afterwards. That is post-decision attitude change, which Brehm demonstrated in 1956 and which this work explicitly sets apart. What Mather and colleagues measured is a source error: a feature is remembered correctly and pinned to the wrong option. Chen and Risen's argument is often assumed to sink this literature too. It does not reach it. Their proof concerns the rate-choose-rate design, where the alternatives appear to spread apart because the choice reveals a preference the ratings measured imprecisely, and no rating spread is measured here. The analogous worry, that people chose the option they already liked, is handled twice. Mather, Shafir and Johnson normalised each score within its scenario so that an option favoured by everybody could not manufacture the effect, and Henkel and Mather found the same bias in people who had been misinformed about which option they picked. The bias tracked the belief, not the choice. The ageing headline is the claim to drop. It rests on one study from 2000, and four later ones looking for the same age difference did not find it.

sources.text: Mather, M., Shafir, E., & Johnson, M. K. (2000). Misremembrance of options past: Source monitoring and choice. Psychological Science, 11(2), 132-138. Source for every number in the evidence section, read from the full text.

Mather, M., & Johnson, M. K. (2000). Choice-supportive source monitoring: Do our decisions seem better to us as we age? Psychology and Aging, 15(4), 596-606. The ageing study; read from a scanned copy.

Mather, M., Shafir, E., & Johnson, M. K. (2003). Remembering chosen and assigned options. Memory & Cognition, 31(3), 422-433. The assignment control, and the paper that states the normalisation used against the preference confound.

Henkel, L. A., & Mather, M. (2007). Memory attributions for choices: How beliefs shape our memories. Journal of Memory and Language, 57(2), 163-176. The false-reminder experiment, read from the full text.

Stoll Benney, K., & Henkel, L. A. (2006). The role of free choice in memory for past decisions. Memory, 14(8), 1001-1011. The best-interest assignment condition; the abstract was read, the full text was not.

Lind, M., Visentini, M., Mäntylä, T., & Del Missier, F. (2017). Choice-supportive misremembering: A new taxonomy and review. Frontiers in Psychology, 8, 2062. The only review of the field, and the source for the ageing failures and the free-recall null.

Chen, M. K., & Risen, J. L. (2010). How choice affects and reflects preferences: Revisiting the free-choice paradigm. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 99(4), 573-594. The artifact argument that applies to rating spread, not to this paradigm; the abstract was read, the full text was not.

Depping, M. K., & Freund, A. M. (2013). When choice matters: Task-dependent memory effects in older adulthood. Psychology and Aging, 28(4), 923-936. The one study in the review reporting no choice-supportive memory after choice; described here as the review describes it, not read.

Queen, T. L., & Hess, T. M. (2010). Age differences in the effects of conscious and unconscious thought in decision making. Psychology and Aging, 25(2), 251-261. One of the studies finding no age difference in choice-supportiveness; listed as the review cites it, not read.

Hess, T. M., & Kotter-Grühn, D. (2011). Social knowledge and goal-based influences on social information processing in adulthood. Psychology and Aging, 26(4), 792-802. Another of the age comparisons; listed as the review cites it, not read.

Hess, T. M., Queen, T. L., & Patterson, T. R. (2012). To deliberate or not to deliberate: Interactions between age, task characteristics, and cognitive activity on decision making. Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 25(1), 29-40. The third age comparison; listed as the review cites it, not read.
